Welcome toDielectric Capacitor

A charged capacitor's gap is filled with a dielectric: what happens to its charge, field and D?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

About: Gauss's law in matter: D follows the free charge, while the bound layer on the dielectric cancels part of it

About this simulation

On screen
The capacitor edge-on, not to scale, with the gap drawn about two fifths of the plate width. The plain signs in the plates (black in the light theme, white in the dark) are the free charge, and eight of them are the 8.85 nC of the empty capacitor at 100 V. Blue signs on the tinted faces of the dashed slab are the bound charge, counted on the same scale. The bold D arrow and the thinner E arrow share one fixed scale: 0.885 µC/m² (D, or ε0E) is one fifth of the gap. The dotted blue pillbox straddles the inner face of the upper plate. The battery is drawn only when it is connected.
Controls
Plates: isolated, or connected to a 100 V battery. Choosing either position starts again from the empty capacitor charged to 100 V, with εr = 1.0. The εr slider sets the relative permittivity of the slab, 1.0 to 4.0 in steps of 0.5; 1.0 is the empty gap. Each change jumps straight to the new equilibrium.
Measured
A = 100 cm² and d = 1.0 mm. Q comes from the capacitance εrε0A/d and the 100 V charging, V = Q/C, and E = V/d. D and the bound density σb come from the linear-dielectric response at that E, and σf = Q/A. The slab is a linear dielectric that fills the gap completely, and the plates are treated as wide enough that the field is uniform. All values are shown to three significant figures, in the Readouts panel below the controls.
Filling a Capacitor with a Dielectric
Parallel-plate capacitor, edge-onfree charge (plain signs), bound charge (blue), D and E

Guided Inquiry

1 · Fill the gap

Keep the switch at isolated plates and εr at 1.0, so that the gap is empty and the plates carry ± 8.85 nC at 100 V. You will raise εr to 2.0. Before you do, predict what appears on the faces of the dielectric next to the plates.

2 · D through the pillbox

Keep the plates isolated and εr at 2.0. The dotted pillbox has its upper face inside the metal of the upper plate and its lower face in the dielectric, so it encloses both the free charge on the plate and the bound layer under it. You will raise εr to 3.0. Before you do, predict the displacement D in the dielectric.

3 · Raise the permittivity again

Keep the plates isolated and εr at 3.0, where E reads 33.3 kV/m. You will raise εr to 4.0. Before you do, predict the field E and the potential difference V.

4 · Connect the battery

Set the switch to connected to the battery, which returns εr to 1.0 with the plates at 100 V and ± 8.85 nC. You will raise εr to 2.0. Before you do, predict what happens to V, E, Q and D.

5 · Free charge against bound charge

Keep the battery connected and εr at 2.0. The free charge density on the positive plate was 0.885 μC/m2 when the gap was empty. You will raise εr to 4.0. Before you do, predict how the free charge added to the positive plate since then, per unit area, compares with the bound charge density on the face of the dielectric next to it.

6 · D, E and the bound charge

D follows the free charge alone: D = σf, whatever the dielectric. E follows all the charge: ε0E = σf + σb, and the bound layer cancels a fraction (εr − 1)/εr of the free charge.

With the plates isolated, Q and D stay fixed while E and V fall by the factor εr. With a battery, V and E stay fixed while Q and D rise by εr. Either way the capacitance is C = εrε0A/d.

Filling a Capacitor with a Dielectric

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A dielectric between capacitor plates does more than multiply the capacitance. This sim draws the free charge on the plates, the charge on the dielectric, and the fields D and E, for isolated plates or plates held at 100 V.

What you'll learn

  • Which charge appears on the faces of the dielectric.
  • Which of D and E follows the free charge.
  • What a battery changes compared with isolated plates.
  • How the free and bound charge compare.
The sim at εr = 1, drawn edge-on and not to scale. A = 100 cm², d = 1.0 mm.

What's on screen

  • Plain signs in the plates are the free charge. Eight of them stand for the 8.85 nC of the empty capacitor at 100 V.
  • Blue signs on the tinted faces of the dashed slab are the bound charge, counted on the same scale. The slab appears once εr is above 1.
  • The bold D arrow and the thinner E arrow run down the gap, from the positive plate towards the negative one.
  • The dotted blue pillbox straddles the inner face of the upper plate. The battery is drawn only when it is connected.

03

The slab faces carry bound charge opposite to the free charge beside them

A linear dielectric polarises in proportion to the total field E in it (notes 3.28): P = ε0χeE, with εr = 1 + χe. In the gap P points from the positive plate towards the negative one, with magnitude (3.33):

P = (χe / εr) σf

P is uniform, so there is no bound volume charge. Bound charge is left only on the two faces. On the face next to the positive plate the outward normal points towards the plate, against P, so σb = −P there, and σb = +P on the face next to the negative plate. Each plate faces a layer of the opposite sign, because the molecules line up with their negative ends towards the positive plate.

At εr = 2, χe = 1, so P = σf/2 = 0.443 µC/m². The face next to the positive plate carries −0.443 µC/m², the other +0.443 µC/m².

The notes' Fig. 29 at εr = 2: free charge in the plates, bound charge (blue) on the faces of the dielectric.
See itRaise εr to 2.0 on isolated plates. Watch for: blue minus signs beside the positive plate, blue plus signs beside the negative one, and σb reading −0.443 µC/m².
04

D equals the free charge density, whatever the dielectric

Gauss's law in matter counts only the free charge (3.27):

∮ D · da = Qf

Take a pillbox of face area Ap whose upper face lies inside the metal plate, where E = 0 and P = 0, so D = 0, and whose lower face lies in the dielectric. D is perpendicular to the plates, so none crosses the curved side. The box encloses σfAp of free charge and also the bound layer under the plate, but only the free charge counts. So DAp = σfAp: the displacement in the dielectric is σf, from the positive plate towards the negative one.

Isolated plates keep Q fixed, so σf = 0.885 µC/m² and D stays at 0.885 µC/m², as in the empty gap, at εr = 2 and at εr = 3. D has no memory of the dielectric. The field does: E = D/εrε0 reads 50.0 kV/m at εr = 2.

The pillbox of the notes' Fig. 29, drawn at the sim's dotted box. D points from the positive plate towards the negative one.
Key idea. D is set by the free charge alone, E by all the charge, free and bound.
See itRaise εr from 2.0 to 3.0 on isolated plates. Watch for: D staying at 0.885 µC/m² while E falls from 50.0 to 33.3 kV/m.
05

With isolated plates E and V fall by the factor εr

Isolated plates hold Q fixed. With D = σf, the field and the potential difference are (3.31):

E = σf / εrε0 , V = Ed = Qd / εrε0A

so the capacitance is C = Q/V = εrε0A/d (3.32), larger by εr. The bound layer explains the fall: the free charge σf and the bound charge −(χe/εr)σf leave σf/εr (3.34), and E is the field of what remains. The bound layer cancels the fraction (εr − 1)/εr of the free charge.

At εr = 3, E = V/d = 33.3 kV/m with V = 33.3 V. At εr = 4, three quarters of the free charge is cancelled: σb = −0.664 µC/m², so E = 25.0 kV/m and V = 25.0 V. Only a conductor would cancel the field completely.

Isolated plates, εr = 1 to 4. The blue part is the free charge cancelled by the bound layer, the grey part is what remains.
See itRaise εr to 4.0 on isolated plates. Watch for: E and V both reading 25.0, and σb reading −0.664 µC/m².
06

With a battery V and E stay put and the free charge grows by the factor εr

A battery holds V fixed, so E = V/d stays at 100 kV/m. The bound layer would lower E, so charge flows onto the plates until the free charge has risen by the factor εr: Q = CV = εrε0AV/d (3.32).

At εr = 2, Q = 17.7 nC, twice the 8.85 nC of the empty capacitor. D follows the free charge, so D = σf = 1.77 µC/m², also doubled, while V and E are unchanged. The battery holds V, not Q.

The larger charge stored at a given potential difference is one reason practical capacitors contain a dielectric. The panel gives both settings at once, computed with the sim's own relations.

plates εr

See itConnect the battery and raise εr to 2.0. Watch for: V and E staying at 100 V and 100 kV/m while Q doubles to 17.7 nC and D to 1.77 µC/m².
07

On a battery the free charge added equals the bound charge

On the battery E = V/d stays at 100 kV/m, so ε0E stays at 0.885 µC/m², the free charge density of the empty gap. The total charge density that produces the field is the free charge plus the bound charge, so

σf + σb = ε0E = 0.885 µC/m²

The free charge is εr times 0.885 and the bound layer, of size (εr − 1) times 0.885, cancels everything above the original 0.885.

Each bit of bound charge is matched by free charge from the battery. At εr = 4, σf = 3.54 µC/m² and σb = −2.66 µC/m². The free charge added since the gap was empty is 2.66 µC/m², the same size as the bound layer, and what remains is 0.885 µC/m².

Isolated plates behave differently: there σb at εr = 4 is only −0.664 µC/m², since it depends on the field, and the field has fallen.

Plates held at 100 V. The added free charge (teal) and the bound charge (blue) are equal in size at every εr.
See itConnect the battery and raise εr to 4.0. Watch for: σf reading 3.54 µC/m² and σb reading −2.66 µC/m²: the free charge added, 2.66, equals the bound charge.
08

Summary

In one line. Free charge, bound charge, D and E in a capacitor filled with a dielectric, followed as εr is raised with the plates isolated or held at 100 V.

Key points

  • The slab's faces carry σb = −P next to the positive plate and +P next to the negative one, P = (χe/εr) σf.
  • D = σf comes from the free charge alone. E follows all the charge.
  • Isolated: Q and D fixed, E and V fall by εr. Battery: V and E fixed, Q and D grow by εr, and the added free charge equals the bound charge.

Common mix-ups

  • "D grows with εr, because D = εrε0E." With isolated plates E falls by the same factor: at εr = 3, E = 33.3 kV/m and D is still 0.885 µC/m².
  • "E and V stay put, because Q has not changed." E follows the bound charge as well. At εr = 4, E = 25.0 kV/m and V = 25.0 V.
  • "The battery holds Q as well as V." It holds V. At εr = 2, Q rises to 17.7 nC.
  • "The dielectric takes charge off the plates." It only polarises, and on the battery Q rises.

Things to try on your own

  • Isolated, εr = 2: name σb, D and E before reading them.
